services.name: Drain Cleaning
services.h1: Drain Cleaning in Round Rock, TX
services.title: Drains | Plumbing Solutions Round Rock, Round Rock, TX
services.meta: Plumbing Solutions Round Rock handles slow, backed-up, and gurgling drains in Round Rock, TX. We inspect the line, clear blockages, and explain access needs.
services.blurb: We clear slow, noisy, backed-up, and odor-producing drains in Round Rock.

paragraphs: A sink that gurgles after it drains, a tub that holds a ring of water, or a floor drain with a sewer smell usually means water is meeting resistance somewhere in the pipe. We check the fixture, trap, branch line, and available cleanout to locate whether the restriction is close to the drain opening or farther along the waste line.

Grease can collect in a kitchen branch, hair and soap residue can narrow a shower line, and wipes or paper can stop a toilet branch even when the bowl itself still flushes. A blockage may also affect more than one fixture: running the washing machine might make water rise in a nearby tub, or an upstairs sink may cause a downstairs drain to gurgle.

A slow single sink can sometimes wait until it becomes a repeat problem, provided water is still draining and there is no wastewater on the floor. A backup, sewer odor, water rising in another fixture, or waste coming through a floor drain should not wait, because a drain blockage can send wastewater into cabinets, tubs, and low areas of the home.

sections.heading: Gurgling drains and sewer odor
paragraphs: Customers often call us about a kitchen sink that drains slowly, a shower pan that fills around their feet, or a toilet that bubbles when the washing machine empties. Other common descriptions are “water comes up in the tub,” “the floor drain smells like sewage,” and “the sink makes a glugging sound after I turn off the faucet.” Each description points us toward a different portion of the drain system.

A single slow bathroom sink can be caused by buildup in the stopper, tailpiece, or trap. A tub that backs up when the toilet flushes can indicate a restriction in the shared branch line, while a sewer odor near a floor drain may come from a dry trap, a vent issue, or waste held in the pipe. Water around a cleanout cap or at the base of a cabinet can also mean the line is blocked beyond the fixture connection.

These symptoms can look alike from the room, but the pipe route, blockage material, and access point can be completely different. We inspect the drain before recommending work because a nearby trap blockage and a deeper line obstruction are separate faults with different labor and equipment needs.

sections.heading: Drain line inspection
paragraphs: At the callout, we start with the affected fixture and ask which drains are slow, which appliances were running when the problem appeared, and whether water has backed up elsewhere. We run water where appropriate, watch the drain level, listen for gurgling, and check the trap, drain opening, cabinet piping, floor drain, and accessible cleanout. A lavatory line is commonly one and one-quarter inches in diameter, while many kitchen, tub, and shower branches use one-and-one-half- or two-inch pipe; the pipe size affects the cable and cutting head we use.

We remove reachable hair, soap residue, food buildup, or debris at the drain opening and use drain-cleaning equipment through the correct access point when the obstruction is farther into the line. A straightforward sink, tub, or shower blockage may take roughly thirty to ninety minutes once we can reach the line. If the drain remains slow after clearing, we may need to inspect farther along the route to identify a damaged pipe, root intrusion, a shifted joint, or buildup beyond the branch.

Most accessible fixture and branch-line blockages can be addressed during the same visit. A buried line, a blocked cleanout, pipe damage behind a wall, or a route that requires excavation is assessed first and scheduled separately so the required access and repair work can be planned correctly.

sections.heading: Pipe access and blockage depth
paragraphs: The location of the blockage matters because a restriction at a sink trap is reached differently from one beyond a wall, under a slab, or out in the yard. An exposed cleanout near the affected line gives us a direct route into the pipe, while a cabinet full of stored items, a sealed access panel, or no visible cleanout can add preparation and diagnostic work.

Pipe material and condition also affect the work. Older cast iron can hold scale along its interior, galvanized pipe can narrow from corrosion, and plastic pipe may have tight fittings or long turns that limit how equipment travels. Grease, hair, paper, mineral buildup, and tree roots each call for a different approach, and recurring stoppages can point to a defect rather than a one-time clog.

The drain route is another factor. A blockage near the fixture generally takes less tracing than one affecting several rooms or a main line, especially when wastewater appears at the lowest drain in the building. If inspection shows a cracked section, a separated joint, or a pipe that needs replacement, we explain the access needed before that additional work is arranged.

sections.heading: Cleanout location and fixture
paragraphs: Before calling, note which room has the slow or backed-up drain and which fixture starts the problem first. Tell us whether the kitchen sink, shower, tub, toilet, washing machine standpipe, or floor drain is involved, and whether another drain reacts when water is used.

If you know where the cleanout is, let us know whether it is in a bathroom, garage, exterior wall, crawl space, or yard. Clear items from under the affected sink or around the floor drain if it is safe to do so, and mention any water that is currently standing in a tub, sink, or shower pan.

It also helps to describe what went into the drain before the stoppage, such as grease, coffee grounds, wipes, hair, or a small object. Call Plumbing Solutions Round Rock at (737) 405-5790 before a backup turns into wastewater coming through a tub, floor drain, or cabinet drain.

services.name: Leak Repair
services.h1: Leak Repair in Round Rock, TX
services.title: Leak Repair | Plumbing Solutions Round Rock | Round Rock, TX
services.meta: Plumbing Solutions Round Rock handles visible and hidden leak repair in Round Rock, TX, tracing damp walls, ceiling stains, pipe drips, and supply-line leaks.
services.blurb: We trace and repair active pipe, valve, and hidden-water leaks in Round Rock.

paragraphs: A drip beneath a sink and a wet spot spreading across a hallway ceiling are both often called a leak, but they are not the same job. A visible drip usually leaves water at a fixture, valve, or supply connection; a hidden leak may show up as a ceiling stain, soft drywall, peeling paint, or a water meter that moves while every tap is off. We trace both the exposed source and the pipe route behind the finished surface.

We check plumbing leaks at kitchens, bathrooms, laundry rooms, garages, ceilings, walls, and outdoor hose connections throughout Round Rock, Brushy Creek, Windemere, and Wells Branch. The source is not always directly above or beside the damp area, since water can run along a pipe, floor joist, cabinet base, or drywall seam before it becomes visible.

An old, dry stain can sometimes wait until the area is inspected and the source is confirmed, but active water, a growing stain, a hissing pipe, or a moving meter should not wait. Water from a pressurized line can soak insulation, swell cabinet panels, damage drywall, and keep feeding a concealed leak even when the visible puddle is small.

sections.heading: Water stain and hissing
paragraphs: Customers often call about a brown ceiling spot, a hissing sound inside a wall, water collecting under a cabinet, or damp carpet along a baseboard. Other common signs include a warm patch on a tile floor, paint bubbling near a shower wall, a musty odor in a closet, or a meter dial that continues to turn after faucets and appliances are off. Each symptom points us toward a different section of pipe, fitting, valve, or drain connection.

A ceiling stain may come from a bathroom supply line above it, while water under a vanity may come from an angle stop, a trap connection, or a split supply hose. A hissing sound can indicate pressurized water escaping, whereas a slow cabinet drip may appear only when a fixture is used. These faults can look similar from the room, but the repair materials, access work, and labor involved are different once we inspect the source.

sections.heading: Pressure test and inspection
paragraphs: During a leak inspection, we start with the visible water path, then check nearby shutoff valves, supply lines, pipe joints, fixture connections, cabinet bases, drywall, and the water meter. We can isolate sections of plumbing, check static and flowing water pressure, and look for pressure changes that point to a supply-side leak. Residential water pressure is generally kept at or below 80 psi; excessive pressure can put added strain on valve seals, braided hoses, and older pipe connections.

A straightforward source trace often takes 30 to 60 minutes when the pipe or fitting is accessible. If we locate an exposed leaking supply line, angle stop, valve, pipe section, or connector and have the appropriate replacement material, that repair is usually handled during the same visit. Repairs requiring a wall opening, ceiling access, a shutoff that will not close, a specialty valve, or a replacement part that must be ordered are scheduled as follow-up work after we identify the route and material.

sections.heading: Pipe access and shutoff valves
paragraphs: The condition of the leaking part affects the scope of repair. A newer braided connector or exposed valve may be replaced without disturbing finished surfaces, while an aging copper joint, galvanized pipe, or damaged line behind tile can require more removal and restoration around the pipe. The material, fitting type, and route from the shutoff to the leak all matter when we determine the repair needed.

Access also changes the work. A cabinet back, access panel, crawlspace opening, ceiling cavity, or wall section may provide a direct path to the line, while a pipe behind a shower surround or finished ceiling requires more strip-back. A seized shutoff valve can prevent isolation at the fixture, and a specialty cartridge, valve body, or matching pipe fitting may need to be ordered before the repair can be completed. If the work involves a permitted alteration or inspection sign-off, that requirement is addressed before the affected plumbing is closed back up.

sections.heading: Fixture plate and access panel
paragraphs: Before calling, note which room has the water and which fixture or wall is closest to the stain, puddle, or sound. If a valve, faucet, appliance connection, or access cover has a make, model, or part number stamped on the body or printed on a label, a clear photo can help us identify the fitting. Let us know whether water is actively running now, whether the main shutoff or local shutoff still operates, and whether the area is behind a cabinet, ceiling, drywall panel, or crawlspace opening. If you know when the fixture or supply line was installed, that age can also help narrow down likely seals, hoses, and valve parts. Call Plumbing Solutions Round Rock at (737) 405-5790 before an active leak enlarges the ceiling stain, damages cabinet material, or soaks the framing around the pipe.

services.name: Water Heater Repair
services.h1: Water Heater Repair in Round Rock, TX
services.title: Plumbing Solutions Round Rock | Round Rock, TX
services.meta: Plumbing Solutions Round Rock handles water heater repair in Round Rock, TX, including cold water, tank leaks, burner faults, and failed heating elements.
services.blurb: Water heater repair for cold water, leaking tanks, and heating faults.

paragraphs: A water heater that takes longer to recover can become a no-hot-water problem after a few more showers, loads of laundry, or dishwasher cycles. Sediment at the bottom of a tank can make popping or rumbling louder over time, while a weak heating element or burner can leave water warm for only a short part of the day.

A small puddle under the tank can also change quickly. Condensation, a pressure-relief valve discharge, a loose connection, and a corroded tank seam can all put water near the drain pan or floor, but they do not call for the same repair. If water reaches a finished wall, cabinet base, or closet flooring, the repair can extend beyond the heater itself.

We repair water heaters for homes in Round Rock, Brushy Creek, Windemere, and Wells Branch from our location at 101 E Old Settlers Blvd. A heater with no hot water, active leakage, a gas odor, or a tripped electrical component should not wait because the tank, burner, element, valve, or surrounding floor can worsen with continued use. A heater that is merely noisy or slow may allow some scheduling flexibility, but it still deserves an inspection before sediment or a worn part causes a larger failure.

sections.heading: Cold water and rumbling
paragraphs: “No hot water” is the most common call, but it can mean a tripped breaker, a failed upper or lower heating element, a thermostat fault, an extinguished pilot, or a burner that will not stay lit. The water may be completely cold, warm only briefly, or hot at one fixture and lukewarm at another.

Customers also call about a rumbling, popping, or knocking sound from the tank. That sound often occurs when sediment collects along the bottom of the tank and traps water beneath it during a heating cycle. A tank can still produce hot water while making that noise, although recovery time may become longer.

Other clear symptoms include rusty or brown water from the hot side, water dripping from the pressure-relief valve pipe, a pilot that repeatedly goes out, or a wet ring around the base of the tank. A gas-fired unit with a sulfur-like gas odor or an electric unit with a burning smell needs to be left off until the source can be checked.

These symptoms can look similar from the kitchen faucet or shower, but they point to different components and different repair work. We inspect the heater before identifying the fault because a valve, element, burner, thermostat, tank, and vent connection do not carry the same parts or labor needs.

sections.heading: Tank and burner inspection
paragraphs: At the visit, we start with the tank, model plate, supply connections, shutoff valve, drain valve, temperature-and-pressure relief valve, and the area around the base. We check whether the tank is actively leaking or whether water is coming from a fitting, relief discharge pipe, condensation line, or drain pan. A basic visual inspection and operating check can often take about 20 to 40 minutes, depending on access and whether the heater is installed in a garage, attic, closet, or utility room.

For an electric water heater, we check the breaker, disconnect, thermostat settings, wiring condition, and heating elements with a meter after the power is isolated. Standard household electric water heaters commonly use a 240-volt circuit, so the electrical side is not something to open or test while energized. For a gas unit, we inspect the pilot or ignition sequence, burner flame, gas control, venting, combustion-air openings, and flue connection.

We can often replace accessible items such as heating elements, thermostats, relief valves, drain valves, thermocouples, igniters, or burner-related components on the same visit when the correct part is available and the tank itself is sound. A replacement tank, a specialty control, a seized shutoff, vent changes, or work requiring an ordered part may need another appointment. When replacement is the sensible route, we explain the condition of the existing heater and the access needed for removal and installation.

sections.heading: Tank age and shutoff valves
paragraphs: The age and condition of the tank are major factors in the repair scope. The manufacturer label usually shows a serial number and model number, and the serial number can help identify the production period. A failed heating element in a sound tank is a different situation from corrosion at the bottom seam or water coming through the tank shell, where replacing a single component will not stop the leak.

Access changes the work as well. A heater in an open garage with a clear path to the water shutoff is usually easier to inspect than one behind a closet door, above a ceiling opening, or in an attic with limited walking space. Drain pans, discharge piping, vent pipes, and nearby framing can add removal or repair steps.

A shutoff valve that will not turn, a corroded connection, or a gas control that must be ordered can expand the job beyond the original fault. We also account for permit or sign-off requirements where applicable, especially when replacement, gas piping, venting, or electrical connections are involved.

sections.heading: Model plate and access
paragraphs: Before calling, look for the model plate on the side of the water heater and note the model number, serial number, fuel type, and tank capacity if they are readable. Tell us whether the heater is in a garage, attic, closet, utility room, or another space, and whether there is a drain pan or standing water below it. If the unit is gas-fired, let us know whether the pilot is out, the burner will not light, or there is any gas odor; if it is electric, note whether a breaker has tripped. It also helps to know whether hot water is absent at every fixture or only at a shower, sink, or appliance. Call Plumbing Solutions Round Rock at (737) 405-5790 before an active tank leak spreads into flooring, walls, or the ceiling below the heater.

services.name: Toilet Repair
services.h1: Toilet Repair in Round Rock, TX
services.title: Toilet Repair | Plumbing Solutions Round Rock | Round Rock, TX
services.meta: Plumbing Solutions Round Rock handles toilet repair in Round Rock, TX, including running tanks, weak flushes, leaks at the base, and faulty fill valves.
services.blurb: We repair running toilets, weak flushes, tank leaks, and loose bases in Round Rock.

paragraphs: A plunger is the sensible first tool when the bowl water rises after a flush. A good seal around the drain opening and several controlled strokes can clear a soft blockage near the trap. It stops helping when the bowl refills without flushing properly, the water level changes on its own, or the problem is in the tank rather than the drain.

We check the parts that make a toilet fill, hold water, and flush: the fill valve, flapper, flush valve seat, handle, chain, tank bolts, and shutoff valve. A worn flapper can let water slip from the tank into the bowl, while a fill valve can keep adding water after the tank should be full. A loose toilet base or water at the floor can point to a failed wax ring, damaged flange, or a crack in the porcelain.

A toilet that only needs a flapper or handle can sometimes wait briefly if the water is shut off at the stop valve and the fixture is not leaking. A toilet with water at the base, an overflowing bowl, or water that will not stop running should not wait, because the floor, subfloor, and surrounding bathroom materials can take on water while the fixture continues to cycle.

sections.heading: Toilet keeps running
paragraphs: “My toilet keeps running” often means the tank refills every few minutes, the fill valve hisses after the flush, or water trickles into the bowl long after the handle has been released. We also hear that the toilet “won’t stop filling,” especially when water reaches the overflow tube inside the tank.

A “weak flush” can be a low tank water level, a slack lift chain, a worn flapper, blocked rim holes, or a partial obstruction in the bowl trap. A toilet that “won’t flush” may have a broken handle, disconnected chain, failed flush valve, or a blockage that a plunger cannot move. Gurgling in the bowl after another fixture drains can also indicate that the issue is beyond the toilet itself.

Water around the toilet base, a rocking bowl, a sewer smell near the floor, and a tank that leaks onto the wall are different symptoms again. These faults can look similar from outside the fixture, but the failed part, labor, and materials can be very different once we inspect the tank, bowl, flange, and shutoff connection.

sections.heading: Toilet inspection
paragraphs: At the fixture, we begin by flushing the toilet and watching the bowl level, tank refill, overflow tube, and water supply connection. We remove the tank lid, inspect the flapper and chain, check whether the fill valve shuts off, and look for cracks, mineral buildup, loose bolts, and moisture around the base. A basic tank and bowl check commonly takes about 15 to 30 minutes, with more time needed when the toilet must be pulled from the floor.

We can measure the water level in relation to the overflow tube and test the shutoff valve before disconnecting the supply line. When a pressure gauge is appropriate, normal residential water pressure is generally kept below 80 psi, since excessive pressure can make fill valves and supply connections cycle or leak. We also check whether the bowl rocks, whether the closet bolts are secure, and whether the flange below the toilet is holding the fixture at the right height.

Flappers, fill valves, handles, chains, supply lines, and some tank bolts are usually the parts we address during the callout when the correct replacement is available. A damaged floor flange, cracked bowl, seized shutoff valve, or a specialty tank component may require a separate booking, particularly when the toilet has to be reset or a matching manufacturer part must be ordered.

sections.heading: Tank parts and shutoff valves
paragraphs: The age and design of the tank parts affect the scope of a repair. A common flapper or universal fill valve is different from a proprietary flush cartridge, an unusual tank-to-bowl gasket, or an older fixture with parts that are no longer widely stocked. A replacement that matches the flush valve opening, tank shape, and manufacturer hardware avoids a repair that does not seal or flush correctly.

Access also changes the work involved. A toilet in a tight water closet, a shutoff valve behind the bowl, corroded closet bolts, or a supply line that cannot be isolated cleanly can add removal and testing work. If the shutoff valve has seized, the flange is damaged under the toilet, or a matching part has to be ordered, the repair can involve more than the tank mechanism. Work involving a changed drain connection or flange condition may also need local sign-off before the fixture is reset.

sections.heading: Tank model and bathroom access
paragraphs: Before calling, check which bathroom contains the toilet and whether it is the only working fixture in that room. The model number may be stamped inside the tank, on the back of the bowl, or beneath the tank lid, and a clear photo of that marking can help us identify the correct flapper, fill valve, or flush valve assembly.

Let us know whether the toilet is running now, whether water is on the floor, and whether the shutoff valve beside the bowl turns. If the toilet rocks, mention whether the floor is tile, vinyl, or another finished surface, since the base and flange may need inspection. Clear access around the tank and bowl helps us reach the supply line, bolts, and floor connection. Call Plumbing Solutions Round Rock at (737) 405-5790 before water at the toilet base spreads into the floor or subfloor.

services.name: Faucet Repair
services.h1: Faucet Repair in Round Rock, TX
services.title: Faucets | Plumbing Solutions Round Rock | Round Rock, TX
services.meta: Plumbing Solutions Round Rock repairs dripping, loose, and leaking faucets in Round Rock, TX, with fixture checks, cartridge diagnosis, and clear next steps.
services.blurb: We repair dripping, loose, noisy, and leaking faucets across Round Rock.

paragraphs: We hear from homeowners when the kitchen faucet “won’t shut off,” the bathroom handle has gone loose, or there is “a little puddle” beneath the sink cabinet. Those descriptions matter because a faucet can leak from the spout, around the handle, below the escutcheon plate, or at a supply connection, and each location points us toward a different part.

A drip from the spout usually leads us to the cartridge, stem, washer, or valve seat. Water collecting around the handle can come from worn O-rings or a damaged cartridge seal. A wet cabinet floor may involve the faucet base, mounting hardware, supply line, or shutoff valve rather than the spout itself, so we inspect the fixture before deciding which repair fits.

A faucet that gives an occasional drip can generally be planned for repair, but a faucet that runs continuously, leaks into a cabinet, or will not turn off should not wait. Water from a faucet leak can damage the cabinet base, loosen mounting hardware, stain the countertop edge, and keep the water meter moving even when no fixture is being used.

sections.heading: Dripping tap and loose handle
paragraphs: “My faucet keeps dripping” is one of the most common calls, whether the drops come from a kitchen spout or a bathroom basin faucet after the handle is off. We also hear that the handle turns too far, spins without changing the water flow, squeaks when moved, or has become hard to turn. A whistling or chattering sound can show up when water passes a worn cartridge, clogged aerator, loose washer, or restricted supply connection.

Another call starts with water appearing at the counter around the faucet base, on the sink rim, or inside the vanity cabinet. A weak stream from one faucet, uneven hot and cold flow, and a spray pattern that shoots sideways are separate symptoms as well. These faults can look similar from across the room, but the cartridge, O-rings, aerator, mounting seal, and supply connection are different repairs with different parts and labor involved.

sections.heading: Fixture inspection
paragraphs: At the fixture, we begin by running the hot and cold sides, watching the spout, handle, base, and cabinet connections for the leak path. We check the handle movement, identify the faucet make where possible, inspect the aerator for sediment, and test the angle stops before isolating water. When flow or pressure is part of the complaint, we can compare the faucet stream with another fixture and use a gauge where needed; many residential plumbing systems operate in the range of 40 to 80 psi.

A straightforward faucet inspection and common repair often takes 30 to 90 minutes, depending on access to the nuts, supply lines, and shutoff valves. We remove the handle and trim, inspect the cartridge or stem, and replace worn seals, O-rings, a cartridge, or an aerator when the correct component is available. We also tighten the mounting hardware and test the spout and cabinet area after water is restored. If a seized shutoff, corroded supply line, damaged valve body, discontinued cartridge, or replacement fixture requires a special part, we explain what needs to be ordered and arrange the remaining work for another visit.

sections.heading: Cartridge access and shutoffs
paragraphs: The age and type of cartridge are major factors in a faucet repair. A common cartridge, washer, or aerator is usually simpler to identify than a discontinued component or a specialty finish with a brand-specific valve body. A faucet that has been dripping for a long time can also have mineral buildup on the retaining nut, stem, or valve seat, making the strip-down more involved than a recent handle leak.

Access under the sink affects the work as much as the visible faucet does. A clear cabinet with working angle stops allows the fixture to be isolated and tested directly, while a seized shutoff, corroded supply connection, crowded vanity, or damaged cabinet floor adds work before the faucet itself can be repaired. If the valve body is cracked, the mounting deck is damaged, a replacement fixture must be ordered, or building requirements call for sign-off, those conditions change the scope from a component repair to a larger fixture job.

sections.heading: Model number and fixture
paragraphs: Before calling, note which room and which faucet has the problem, such as the kitchen sink, primary bathroom basin, laundry sink, or bar sink. If you have the installation sheet, box, receipt, or a tag from the fixture, the model number and make can help us identify the correct cartridge or handle parts. A clear photo of the spout, handles, logo, and area beneath the sink is useful when the model number is not available. Let us know roughly how old the faucet is, whether water is running now, and whether the cabinet has clear access to the shutoff valves. Mention any wobble at the faucet base or water on the cabinet floor so we can prepare for the mounting hardware and connections involved. Call Plumbing Solutions Round Rock at (737) 405-5790 before a steady drip wears the cartridge further or a cabinet leak swells the wood beneath the sink.

services.name: Garbage Disposal Repair
services.h1: Garbage Disposal Repair in Round Rock, TX
services.title: Plumbing Solutions Round Rock | Round Rock, TX
services.meta: Plumbing Solutions Round Rock repairs garbage disposals in Round Rock, TX, including humming motors, sink backups, leaks, and under-sink inspections.
services.blurb: Humming, leaking, or jammed disposal repair for Round Rock kitchens.

paragraphs: Older kitchens around Round Rock often have a disposal, drain elbow, dishwasher hose, and outlet packed into the same sink cabinet. We see trouble where an aging mounting ring has loosened, a hard object has reached the grinding chamber, or years of food residue have collected around the splash guard and drain opening. Homes in Brushy Creek, Windemere, and Wells Branch can have the same issue whether the kitchen has a stainless-steel sink or an older composite basin.

A disposal is not a place for grease, stringy vegetables, bones, coffee grounds, or utensils, but a stoppage does not always mean something is trapped in the chamber. A humming motor may have a jammed flywheel, while water at the cabinet base may come from the discharge gasket, dishwasher inlet, sink flange, or the disposal housing itself. We inspect the unit, the P-trap, and the connections below the sink before recommending a repair or replacement.

A disposal that is silent or humming without a leak can usually stay unused until we inspect it. Water beneath the cabinet, a cracked housing, or a backup that rises into the sink should not wait, because leaking discharge water can swell the cabinet floor and a blocked disposal can force dirty water back through the sink.

sections.heading: Humming disposal and sink odor
paragraphs: Customers often call us because the garbage disposal hums but will not spin, the unit will not turn on, or the sink fills with water when the switch is flipped. Other common descriptions are a grinding noise after a spoon or bottle cap fell inside, water dripping from the bottom of the disposal, and a sour odor that returns after the kitchen sink is rinsed. We also hear about a disposal that runs but leaves food in the basin, or a dishwasher that drains into a sink that suddenly backs up.

A hum can point to a jammed grinding plate, seized bearings, or a motor that no longer starts. A bad odor may come from the splash guard, food debris in the chamber, a slow drain line, or water held in the trap. A leak at the top mounting assembly is different from a leak at the discharge tube or a split disposal body, even when all three leave water in the same cabinet. These symptoms can look alike from the kitchen floor, but they involve different parts, labor, and charges once we inspect the sink cabinet.

sections.heading: Under-sink inspection
paragraphs: During an under-sink inspection, we first disconnect power where needed and check the reset button, wall switch, outlet, cord, and visible wiring connection. We look inside the grinding chamber with a light, check the splash guard, and test whether the grinding plate turns freely with the proper tool. We then fill the sink, run water through the disposal, and inspect the mounting ring, sink flange, dishwasher inlet, discharge elbow, trap, and drain pipe for movement or leaks.

We also check whether the unit fits the usual 3 1/2-inch sink opening and whether the discharge connection aligns with the existing drain pipe. A basic inspection and jam clearing commonly takes about 20 to 40 minutes, while changing a disposal can take longer when the mount, wiring, or drain route needs adjustment. A reset, accessible jam, loose mounting hardware, worn gasket, or reachable discharge connection is often handled during the visit when the needed part is available. A replacement requiring a special mounting assembly, a nonstandard electrical connection, cabinet repair, or an ordered part is booked as follow-up work.

sections.heading: Motor age and cabinet access
paragraphs: The age and condition of the motor make a major difference in the scope of disposal work. A newer unit with a lodged utensil or tripped reset may need clearing and testing, while an older unit with seized bearings, a cracked body, or a failed motor may make replacement more practical. The model can also determine whether a splash guard, stopper, mounting ring, or discharge gasket can be replaced separately.

Cabinet access affects the work when the disposal is tightly surrounded by water filters, pull-out shelves, stored cleaners, dishwasher hoses, or drain piping. A corroded mounting ring, stuck discharge nut, damaged flange, or seized dishwasher supply valve can add work before the disposal can be removed or reconnected. If the correct model-specific part must be ordered, that changes the repair plan from a straightforward visit to a return installation. Electrical alterations or changes to a dishwasher connection can also require additional review when local approval or another trade is involved.

sections.heading: Model plate and sink cabinet
paragraphs: Before calling, find the model number on the disposal label, usually printed on the side or underside of the unit near the motor housing. Tell us which kitchen sink has the problem, roughly when the disposal was installed, and whether the unit hums, leaks, drains slowly, or does nothing when the switch is used. If water is present, note whether it is coming from the top mounting area, the discharge elbow, the dishwasher hose, or the bottom of the housing. Clear stored items from the sink cabinet if possible so we can reach the outlet, reset button, drain pipe, and mounting assembly. Call Plumbing Solutions Round Rock at (737) 405-5790 if water is leaking from the disposal body or discharge connection, because that water can damage the cabinet base and flooring beneath the sink.

about: We work from 101 E Old Settlers Blvd in Round Rock, TX, and cover homes and businesses in Round Rock, Brushy Creek, Windemere, and Wells Branch. Our plumbing work begins with a call about the room, fixture, or pipe involved.

We take on drain cleaning, leak repair, water heater repair, toilet repair, faucet repair, and garbage disposal repair. We repair and replace plumbing fixtures and equipment in kitchens, bathrooms, utility rooms, and other areas of the property.

At the start of a visit, we look at the affected fixture, nearby pipes, shutoff valve, drain line, and visible water or damage. We check the location of the issue before discussing the work and any cost, based on what we find at the property.
